rv.q: Rob Ashford's production is very classy indeed and worth it for the design alone. It's a very enjoyable tribute, beautifully staged.
If you want to see a really fine play… well, two out of three ain't bad.
A terrific, poignant performance and a set that deserves applause of its own, but the play itself doesn't quite fill the space.
Here is a particularly frustrating example of an at least five-star performance of an at best three-star script.

Ferguson, slouching and perma-hungover in a racoon coat and white hat, looks little like Capote, who resembled a white-blond, moon-faced, devil child. But he captures his insinuating, conspiratorial prattle and his vaunting self-belief.
For all Tyler Ferguson's magnetism, Tru is too brittle, bitchy and self-interested to care much about.
In the end, watching Tru is a bit like attending a party full of strangers and spending the whole evening wondering exactly why one bothered.
Tru is a magnificent production, guided by Rob Ashford’s direction and anchored by Tyler Ferguson’s faultless performance.
Jesse Tyler Ferguson, best known for his role in Modern Family, seems born to play the role.

Tru delivers a beautifully realised evening in the company of one of the great wits of the last century, led by an understatedly magnetic Ferguson and housed in a remarkable set that puts you right inside Capote's apartment.
This play may not offer anything new, but it is a star vehicle, and Ferguson does not disappoint.
Ashford has chosen to make this element of the script explicit, to great effect.
Ferguson's rich and dynamic individual performance soars in an engrossing delivery that never falters.
Tru is a chance to see a performer at the top of their game and to be blown away by their sheer magnificence.
Staging TRU in such intimate fashion gives the audience a front-row seat into a world of royal scandal and power couple infidelities that plays on much that still feels relevant to today's world.
Ultimately, Truman Capote is a alcoholic, name-dropping narcissist, and Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s portrayal of him is brilliant.

cn.t: Ferguson delivers a captivating performance in a stunning immersive set, but critics find Allen's 1989 monologue script thin and dated, making for an uneven production that prioritizes style over substance.
